analysis.investment_thesis: Gravita is a legitimate recycling business with 9 years of consecutive profits and manageable debt, but at P/E 31.7x and P/B 5.29x the market price of INR 1,641 demands nearly triple the Graham Number of ~INR 548 — there is no margin of safety whatsoever. The intelligent investor does not pay a speculative premium for past growth, however impressive.
key_strengths: Nine consecutive years of positive net profits (2016–2025), with CAGR of 58.4% — demonstrating durable earning power
Debt/Equity of only 0.20 and interest coverage ~7.6x (EBITDA 348 Cr / Finance Cost 46 Cr) — a clean balance sheet that can survive adversity
Revenue nearly 9x over the decade (430→3,869 Cr) in a structurally sound secondary-metal recycling business with ESG tailwinds
key_risks: Valuation is indefensible by any Graham metric: P/E 31.7x (limit: 15), P/B 5.29x (limit: 1.5), trading at 3× the Graham Number — the price already reflects many years of optimistic growth
Other Income (INR 111 Cr in FY25) represents ~35% of net profit (313 Cr) — quality of earnings is suspect when a large slice comes from non-operating sources
Free cash flow is erratic and frequently negative (-61 Cr in FY22, -56 Cr in FY24); operating cash conversion is inconsistent despite reported profits
red_flags: Equity surged from INR 837 Cr (FY24) to INR 2,260 Cr (FY25) — a near-tripling via apparent large equity issuance, massively diluting existing shareholders
Graham Number ≈ INR 548 (√[22.5 × EPS ~43 × BVPS ~310]); current price INR 1,641 implies a 200% premium with zero margin of safety
Other income of INR 88–111 Cr in recent years inflates reported profitability — stripping it out reduces FY25 net profit materially
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Gravita passes the qualitative smell test that most companies fail: it has a real, capital-intensive business recycling lead, aluminium, and plastic scrap, a 30-year operating history, promoter holding above 55%, and a debt load so modest (D/E 0.20) that insolvency risk is remote. The interest coverage of 7.6x clears my 3.5x threshold comfortably. These are the bones of a sound enterprise. However, Mr. Market is demanding an extraordinary price for them — P/E of 31.7, P/B of 5.29, and EV/EBITDA of 24.5 all violate every quantitative filter I have established over a lifetime of study. My Graham Number calculation yields approximately INR 548; the stock trades at INR 1,641, a 200% premium. Paying three times intrinsic value requires the business to execute flawlessly for years just to justify today's price — that is speculation dressed in a business suit.

Two additional concerns weigh heavily. First, "Other Income" of INR 111 Cr in FY25 accounts for roughly 35% of the reported net profit of INR 313 Cr. An intelligent investor must ask: what is this income, and is it recurring? Elevated other income in FY23 (88 Cr) and FY24 (76 Cr) suggests it may include forex gains, investments, or subsidiary dividends — none of which belong in an assessment of core earning power. Second, the equity base nearly tripled in a single year (FY24→FY25, from 837 Cr to 2,260 Cr), indicating a large capital raise that dilutes older shareholders. Free cash flow has been negative in two of the last four years. I do not doubt this is a growing business; I doubt the buyer at today's price is investing rather than speculating.
